question: Besides body movement, what is another vital function of skeletal muscle?

options.A: Regulating blood pH through bicarbonate storage
options.B: Filtering metabolic waste products from the blood
options.C: Producing red blood cells for oxygen transport
options.D: Generating body heat to maintain core temperature

explanation: Muscle contraction requires energy, and much of that energy is released as heat, which helps keep the body warm. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T9#GNS121_U3_T9_h1)

question: What is a major risk of relying on virtual health communities?

options.A: Members are legally required to pay monthly subscription fees
options.B: Unverified medical advice and misinformation can spread rapidly
options.C: Patients will completely lose access to their local doctors
options.D: It guarantees that patients will never experience illness again

explanation: Spot on! Anyone can post online, so fake news and harmful health remedies can easily trick people if they aren't careful.

question: What is the process of assigning numbers to qualitative categories called?

options.A: Data coding
options.B: Data graphing
options.C: Data cleaning
options.D: Data scaling

explanation: Coding is the translation of descriptive categories into numerical codes to make computer entry and statistical analysis straightforward. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h3)

question: A nurse feels stressed because personal values clash with an assigned care duty. What type of conflict is this?

options.A: Intrapersonal conflict
options.B: Interpersonal conflict
options.C: Intragroup conflict
options.D: Intergroup conflict

explanation: When the battle is inside your own head regarding your values and duties, it's an intrapersonal conflict. You've got this!

question: Why is it often so hard to enforce anti-FGM laws at the local community level?

options.A: Federal laws completely override all state and local police actions
options.B: Traditional rulers are legally permitted to bypass state courts
options.C: Medical doctors are required by law to perform the procedure instead
options.D: Cultural secrecy and fear of ostracization prevent people from reporting cases

explanation: That's right. Because FGM is deeply rooted in some cultures, families keep it a secret and are terrified of speaking out or reporting offenders.

question: Which of these is NOT a serious warning sign covered by the ACHES mnemonic?

options.A: Severe pain and swelling in the lower leg
options.B: Mild morning nausea and mild breast tenderness
options.C: Severe chest pain and shortness of breath
options.D: Sudden severe headaches with visual disturbances

explanation: Mild nausea and tender breasts are normal, everyday side effects when starting hormones. ACHES is meant to catch the rare, serious red flags!

question: How can you keep hands clean in a clinic when the running water supply stops?

options.A: Use set-up handwashing stations like Veronica buckets and alcohol rubs
options.B: Wipe hands clean with ordinary office paper towels
options.C: Wear the same pair of examination gloves all day long
options.D: Skip handwashing until municipal water lines are fully restored

explanation: Brilliant! Improvised running-water setups like Veronica buckets and alcohol-based rubs keep patient care safe even when the taps go dry.

question: What is a key sign that a baby has pathological jaundice instead of normal physiological jaundice?

options.A: The baby feeding well and crying with a strong voice
options.B: Yellow skin fading completely by the end of the second week
options.C: Yellow color appearing within the first 24 hours of life
options.D: Jaundice showing up strictly on the third day after birth

explanation: Normal physiological jaundice takes a little time to show up. Any yellow color appearing on day one (within 24 hours) is a red flag that needs a closer look by the medical team.

question: You notice false health rumors spreading rapidly during a disease outbreak. What is the best action to take?

options.A: Ignore the rumors because they will eventually fade away
options.B: Report the community members spreading rumors to the police
options.C: Actively communicate correct safety updates and debunk the rumors
options.D: Wait for international health organizations to issue a formal ban

explanation: Well done! Addressing misinformation directly prevents panic and keeps people focused on accurate health actions.

question: A mum who delivered an hour ago at a primary clinic has soaked three maternity pads in 30 minutes and feels dizzy. What's going on?

options.A: An impending eclamptic seizure
options.B: Normal postpartum lochia flow
options.C: A normal physiological recovery sign
options.D: Primary postpartum hemorrhage

explanation: Soaking pads rapidly plus dizziness means heavy bleeding (PPH). She needs quick intervention right away!

question: Which nursing action is a must when managing a timed suppression test?

options.A: Stopping all patient monitoring once the initial baseline is drawn
options.B: Administering the suppression medication at random convenient times
options.C: Ensuring blood samples are drawn at the exact prescribed intervals
options.D: Allowing the patient to eat high-sugar meals during the test procedure

explanation: Precision is everything here! Dynamic tests rely completely on exact timing to track how hormone levels change after giving a medication.

question: How often do doctors usually check TSH levels when figuring out the right levothyroxine dose?

options.A: Every single day before the morning dose
options.B: Only once every five years
options.C: Every six to eight weeks until stable
options.D: Every twenty-four hours in the acute ward

explanation: Because the drug takes time to build up and settle in the body, doctors wait 6 to 8 weeks before checking the blood to see if the dose is spot on.

question: What is a community health nurse's main job inside a flood relief camp?

options.A: Managing federal budgets for national security operations
options.B: Preventing disease outbreaks by promoting hygiene and managing basic health issues
options.C: Conducting police investigations into the cause of the flood
options.D: Constructing permanent concrete housing for all displaced families

explanation: You got it, nurse! In relief camps, keeping hygiene high and treating minor sicknesses stops outbreaks like cholera before they start.

question: What is the proper way to remove a honeybee stinger stuck in the skin?

options.A: Scrape it gently across the skin using a flat, rigid edge
options.B: Burn the stinger with a heated match to neutralize the venom
options.C: Squeeze the venom sac tightly with metal tweezers and pull straight out
options.D: Scrub the area vigorously with a stiff surgical brush

explanation: Never squeeze a bee stinger! Squeezing pushes more venom into the skin. Instead, gently scrape it away with something flat like a card.

question: How does gastroenteritis fundamentally affect the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: It blocks the bile ducts and stops liver enzyme production
options.B: It creates permanent ulcers in the lower esophageal sphincter
options.C: It permanently destroys the muscular wall of the large bowel
options.D: It causes inflammation of the stomach and intestinal lining

explanation: The core pathological feature of gastroenteritis is the acute inflammation of the mucous membranes inside the stomach and intestines. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h1)

question: What term is used when a reflex response is completely missing?

options.A: Autonomic dysreflexia
options.B: Neuromuscular fatigue
options.C: Hyperreflexia
options.D: Areflexia

explanation: Areflexia means the reflex is absent ('a-' meaning without). If it's just very weak, we call it hyporeflexia. You've got this!

question: Why is it super helpful for nurses to understand basic X-ray imaging?

options.A: To replace the radiologist in reading films
options.B: To prescribe the correct radiation dosage
options.C: To operate the heavy X-ray machine safely
options.D: To help coordinate care and ease patient anxiety

explanation: As a nurse, you are the friendly face who prepares patients and calms their nerves before procedures. Great nursing starts with great communication!

question: Which of the following is an example of non-verbal communication that can significantly influence a patient interaction?

options.A: The specific medical terminology used in the care plan
options.B: Open posture and relaxed facial expressions
options.C: A printed schedule of clinic operating hours
options.D: The speed at which discharge instructions are read aloud

explanation: Body language, posture, and facial expressions are non-verbal cues that convey openness, empathy, or disinterest without using words. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T23#GNS225_U2_T23_h2)

question: Why do nurses need to check a patient's other medications when starting an antiparasitic drug that goes through the liver?

options.A: Liver enzymes completely neutralize the therapeutic effect of all parasites
options.B: Patients with liver issues cannot absorb any form of topical cream
options.C: Many antiparasitic drugs are metabolized by liver enzymes, altering blood levels
options.D: Hepatic enzymes prevent gastrointestinal side effects entirely

explanation: The liver handles many of these drugs. If another medicine speeds up or slows down those liver enzymes, it can accidentally cause drug toxicity or make the treatment fail.

question: Why do doctors prescribe multiple antibiotics at once to treat an H. pylori infection?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing common side effects
options.B: To speed up the healing time of the skin across the abdomen
options.C: To prevent the bacterium from developing resistance to single drug therapies
options.D: To replace the intrinsic factor lost during chronic inflammation

explanation: You got it! H. pylori is tough, so combining drugs stops the bacteria from outsmarting a single antibiotic and clears the infection completely.

question: Why does a cold swimming pool stop feeling so freezing after you stay in it for a few minutes?

options.A: The skin stops conducting heat away from internal organs.
options.B: Thermoreceptors adapt to the constant temperature over time.
options.C: Cold receptors completely destroy themselves upon prolonged exposure.
options.D: Blood circulation to the superficial skin increases rapidly.

explanation: Exactly right! This is called sensory adaptation—your thermoreceptors simply slow down their firing rate when a temperature stays the same.

question: Why do patients with these disorders sometimes show sudden changes like anger or unfriendliness (apathy)?

options.A: Temporary side effects from routine physical therapy sessions
options.B: Inadequate daily fluid intake causing mild dehydration
options.C: Normal psychological adjustment to aging processes
options.D: Damage to frontal lobe structures controlling mood and behavior

explanation: The frontal lobe is like our brain's emotional dashboard. When it gets damaged, managing moods becomes really tough for the patient.

question: Why is teamwork among different healthcare professionals so crucial in long-term care?

options.A: Medical doctors require assistance to perform basic personal hygiene
options.B: Residents typically have multiple complex physical, emotional, and social needs
options.C: It ensures that nurses never have to communicate with resident families
options.D: It removes the need for documenting resident care assessments

explanation: Brilliant! Because residents have varied needs, nurses, doctors, dietitians, and therapists must work hand-in-hand to cover all bases.

question: What is the main trap when relying on routine blood tests to check mineral levels like calcium or magnesium?

options.A: Labs cannot measure minerals accurately in human blood.
options.B: Mineral levels change drastically every five minutes.
options.C: Blood levels may stay normal even when tissue stores are low.
options.D: Minerals break down instantly when exposed to room air.

explanation: The body is smart—it will pull minerals out of your bones and tissues to keep the blood levels looking normal, which can easily trick you!

question: Why are older adults especially vulnerable to bad reactions from medications?

options.A: Their liver and kidneys clear medications much more slowly
options.B: They always take their medicines at the wrong time of day
options.C: Their stomachs absorb all drugs faster than younger adults
options.D: They refuse to drink water when swallowing pills

explanation: As we age, our liver and kidneys slow down. Because they clear drugs more slowly, the medication stays in the older person's body longer and can build up to toxic levels.

question: In the context of vulnerable families, what is 'property grabbing'?

options.A: Community members stealing food donations meant for orphans
options.B: Relatives seizing land and belongings after a parent dies
options.C: The government confiscating hospital records of deceased patients
options.D: Banks freezing accounts belonging to children under age eighteen

explanation: Property grabbing happens when greedy relatives unlawfully chase away a grieving widow and her children to take over their home and properties. It's a harsh reality nurses should be aware of to guide families.

question: Why is it important for an objective to be 'Achievable' rather than impossible to reach?

options.A: To stretch the team without causing exhaustion and burnout.
options.B: To make sure work is completed twice as fast.
options.C: To ensure the hospital avoids spending any money at all.
options.D: To eliminate the need for any staff supervision.

explanation: We want goals that challenge us to grow, but setting impossible bars only leads to frustration and burnout. Balance is key!

question: A patient refuses malaria treatment because they feel the drugs are too expensive and far away. In the Health Belief Model, what is this called?

options.A: Perceived severity
options.B: Perceived barriers
options.C: Perceived benefits
options.D: Perceived susceptibility

explanation: Perceived barriers are the hurdles, costs, or inconveniences that make someone hesitant to take healthy actions.

question: Why might a rural village suddenly see vitamin deficiencies during the heavy rainy season?

options.A: Excessive rainfall causing an overabundance of fresh meat in local stores
options.B: Villagers deliberately choosing to fast from fruits and vegetables during rainstorms
options.C: Washed-out roads cutting off transport of fresh produce from regional markets
options.D: Soil contamination making all locally grown crops completely poisonous

explanation: Bad weather washes out roads, isolating communities so fresh, perishable foods can't get delivered.

question: Who is the primary audience for hospital in-service training sessions?

options.A: Secondary school students interested in science careers
options.B: Local nursing staff and clinical teams working on the wards
options.C: Government ministers responsible for national taxation
options.D: International scholars attending academic symposiums abroad

explanation: In-service training aims directly at the frontline healthcare workers who deliver daily patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U4_T2#GNS224_U4_T2_h4)

question: What makes a mouth sore suspicious for oral cancer rather than a normal, everyday canker sore?

options.A: It is extremely painful when eating citrus
options.B: It appears directly on the tip of the tongue
options.C: It goes away and returns every few months
options.D: It fails to heal within two weeks

explanation: As a rule of thumb in nursing, any sore in the mouth that hangs around for more than two weeks needs a closer look and a possible biopsy.

question: Which samples are most commonly used to collect DNA for a pharmacogenetic test?

options.A: A simple cheek swab or blood draw
options.B: A deep dermal skin punch biopsy
options.C: A routine 24-hour urine collection
options.D: A sterile cerebrospinal fluid sample

explanation: You got it! Testing your DNA is quick and painless, usually requiring just a simple blood sample or a gentle swab inside your cheek. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T5#GNS125_U1_T5_h6)

question: A nurse needs a quick estimate of a patient's daily calorie needs without special gas-exchange equipment. What is best to use?

options.A: A validated predictive equation like the Mifflin-St Jeor formula
options.B: A laboratory blood test measuring thyroid antibody levels
options.C: A direct calorimetry thermal chamber room
options.D: A 24-hour continuous core body temperature recording

explanation: When fancy equipment isn't around, clinical formulas using age, weight, and height give us a fast, reliable estimate of calorie needs.

question: Which statement correctly describes the link between correlation and causation?

options.A: Variables that are correlated must have a causal link
options.B: Correlation does not prove causation
options.C: Correlation always proves direct causation
options.D: Causation is required to calculate a correlation coefficient

explanation: Remember this golden rule of research: just because two things move together doesn't mean one caused the other! Great job.

question: Why is it so important for nurses to check for drug interactions between ART and other medications?

options.A: Other medications will instantly turn HIV into a completely different virus
options.B: Patients are forbidden from taking pain relief while on ARVs
options.C: Liver enzyme interactions can dangerously lower or raise drug levels in the blood
options.D: Taking two pills at once causes them to physically dissolve in the throat

explanation: Spot on! ARVs interact with liver enzymes. If we aren't careful, another drug can accidentally wash the ARVs out too fast or build them up to toxic levels.

question: Why is a budget considered such an important financial tool?

options.A: It provides a clear benchmark to compare actual spending against planned goals
options.B: It automatically generates profits without requiring staff work
options.C: It gives nurse managers unlimited power to hire any staff they want
options.D: It stops patients from ever questioning their hospital bills

explanation: A budget sets a clear target so managers can check whether the unit is staying on track or spending too much.

question: Which of the following is NOT a routine component of a comprehensive clinical assessment for a febrile patient?

options.A: Monitoring respiratory and pulse rates
options.B: Checking the level of consciousness
options.C: Measuring daily bone mineral density
options.D: Observing skin warmth and diaphoresis

explanation: Bone density measurements are unrelated to the acute assessment of a febrile illness. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T6#GNS123_U3_T6_h5)

question: What practice helps germs develop resistance to chemical disinfectants?

options.A: Allowing alcohol-based hand rubs to air-dry completely on the skin
options.B: Changing cleaning cloths and disinfecting solutions after every single room
options.C: Washing hands with soap and water after caring for every infectious patient
options.D: Using disinfectants at too weak a dilution or cutting down the required contact time

explanation: You nailed it! If a disinfectant is too weak or wiped away too early, the tougher germs survive and learn to resist the chemical over time.

question: What is the main purpose of an incident report in a healthcare facility?

options.A: To provide permanent legal evidence for the patient's court case
options.B: To document safety events and improve institutional systems
options.C: To formally punish the specific nurse who made the mistake
options.D: To calculate the daily patient feeding and laundry costs

explanation: Incident reports aren't for witch hunts! They are learning tools to help the hospital spot recurring issues and make the ward safer for everyone.

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for stimulating the gallbladder to release bile?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Gastrin
options.C: Secretin
options.D: Cholecystokinin

explanation: Cholecystokinin is released when fats and proteins enter the small intestine, prompting the gallbladder to contract and release stored bile. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which health issue is closely linked to heavy metal exposure from bad toxic waste disposal?

options.A: Neurological damage
options.B: Seasonal allergies
options.C: Vision improvement
options.D: Muscle hypertrophy

explanation: That's correct! Toxic metals like lead and mercury attack the nervous system, leading to serious brain and developmental issues.

question: Why does passing urine normally help protect your body from infections?

options.A: It physically flushes out bacteria before they can stick to the tract
options.B: It coats the bladder wall with a thick protective mucous layer
options.C: It neutralizes the pH of the urine to stop bacterial growth
options.D: It increases the core body temperature to kill pathogens

explanation: Think of regular urination like a natural tap flush! It sweeps invading germs out of the system before they can settle down and cause trouble.

question: A nurse picks up a sterile surgical tray from the supply room and notices the outer paper wrapper is damp. What should she do?

options.A: Dry the outside wrapper carefully with a clean towel and use it
options.B: Check the chemical indicator strip and use the tray if the color changed
options.C: Consider the item contaminated and return it for re-sterilization
options.D: Open the package immediately before the moisture spreads further

explanation: Moisture on packaging acts like a sponge, pulling bacteria right through the barrier. It's best to safely reprocess it!

question: A baker who develops sudden wheezing and chest tightness after inhaling flour dust at work is most likely suffering from which condition?

options.A: Asbestos-related pleural plaque
options.B: Occupational asthma
options.C: Bacterial lobar pneumonia
options.D: Coal worker's pneumoconiosis

explanation: Exposure to organic sensitizers like flour triggers an allergic airway response characterized by bronchospasm, which defines occupational asthma. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h3)

question: How do chemical messengers like cytokines cause those early signs of illness when the incubation period ends?

options.A: They destroy the pathogen's cell wall completely
options.B: They stop the pathogen from entering the bloodstream
options.C: They block nerve signals so the patient feels no pain
options.D: They provoke inflammatory responses that cause visible symptoms

explanation: Great job! These chemical messengers trigger inflammation, which is why you end up with fevers and body aches.

question: Which of these is a major threat that can crash a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Issuing drugs on informal credit to friends and colleagues
options.B: Keeping the pharmacy windows open for ventilation
options.C: Writing clear dosage instructions on drug packs
options.D: Conducting weekly physical counts of medicine boxes

explanation: Giving drugs out on 'friendship credit' drains the cash drawer fast, making it impossible to restock. Business and friendly favors don't mix here!

question: A pregnant woman having severe pre-eclampsia seizures is most likely to be given which mineral drug?

options.A: Atropine drops
options.B: Magnesium sulfate
options.C: Ferrous sulfate
options.D: Quinine tablets

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is a vital mineral medication given via IV to stop and prevent dangerous seizures in pre-eclampsia.

question: Why is it important for nurses to ask direct questions about hopelessness to clients with chronic illness?

options.A: To uncover hidden thoughts of depression or self-harm early
options.B: To make the client stop talking about their physical pain
options.C: To prove to the doctor that the client has a psychiatric disorder
options.D: To fill out the hospital admission paperwork faster

explanation: Directly asking about emotional pain allows nurses to protect vulnerable clients and provide timely mental health support. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T5#GNS222_U3_T5_h5)

question: How does foremilk differ from hindmilk during a single feed?

options.A: Foremilk is more watery, while hindmilk contains higher amounts of fat
options.B: Foremilk has high calorie counts, while hindmilk contains only lactose
options.C: Foremilk is produced at night, while hindmilk is produced during the day
options.D: Foremilk contains antibodies, while hindmilk contains only pure water

explanation: Spot on! Foremilk quenches the baby's thirst at the start, while the rich, creamy hindmilk follows to help them grow and feel full.

question: Which of the following is a primary goal of conducting epidemiological studies?

options.A: Replacing bedside clinical nurses with data entry clerks
options.B: Eliminating the need for patient consent in research trials
options.C: Providing a foundation for public health policy and disease control
options.D: Ensuring that all hospitals maintain identical financial budgets

explanation: Epidemiology isn't just about numbers—it gives health leaders the real-world evidence they need to build strong health policies and stop outbreaks.

question: What happens in a Type I error during research?

options.A: Rejecting a true null hypothesis, creating a false positive
options.B: Using a sample size that is far too large for the hospital ward
options.C: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis, creating a false negative
options.D: Forgetting to calculate the mean before publishing a research paper

explanation: A Type I error is like getting a false alarm—you mistakenly think your new intervention works wonders, but it's actually just random chance.

question: What does 'resource mobilisation' mainly mean in community health nursing?

options.A: Hiring expensive foreign experts to run local clinics
options.B: Waiting for international organizations to send free cash
options.C: Closing down rural health centers to save money
options.D: Identifying and gathering available local and outside resources

explanation: You nailed it! Resource mobilisation is all about pulling together the people, materials, and funds needed to make the health plan happen.

question: A patient is taking extra fiber for constipation. What important advice must you give them?

options.A: Increase fluid intake significantly alongside the extra fiber
options.B: Take the fiber supplement immediately before going to bed
options.C: Cook all high-fiber vegetables until they are completely soft
options.D: Eliminate all fats from the diet to make the fiber work faster

explanation: Well done! Fiber acts like a sponge—if patients don't drink enough water with it, it can actually make constipation worse or cause a blockage.

question: How does water move from inside the gut into the bloodstream during oral rehydration?

options.A: It follows sodium and glucose passively via osmosis
options.B: It is pumped across by high-pressure gradients
options.C: It travels through separate channels unaffected by solutes
options.D: It is pushed across by active muscular contractions

explanation: Water loves to follow where solutes go! When sodium and glucose are absorbed into the gut cells, water naturally follows them to keep the balance right.

question: What is the correct way to fix a writing mistake in a paper health register?

options.A: Apply thick correction fluid until the page is blindingly white.
options.B: Scratch it out heavily with a pen until it is totally hidden.
options.C: Draw a single neat line through the mistake, write 'error', and sign beside it.
options.D: Rip out the page and rewrite the whole day's entries.

explanation: Never scribble out or use heavy Tipp-Ex on medical records! A single neat line keeps things legal, honest, and easy to read while showing an official correction was made.

question: What is the golden rule when writing the results section of your research?

options.A: Include your personal opinions on why the treatment failed
options.B: Focus heavily on reviewing what other authors previously wrote
options.C: Present the findings objectively without personal interpretation
options.D: Hide any unexpected data that does not match your original guess

explanation: Just report what the numbers show! Save your opinions and deep thoughts for the discussion section.

question: A nurse sets up a free blood pressure check at the local market. What level of prevention is this?

options.A: Secondary prevention
options.B: Tertiary prevention
options.C: Primary prevention
options.D: Primordial prevention

explanation: You nailed it! Secondary prevention is about catching health issues early through screening before they cause major trouble.

question: Which of the following best describes continuous quality improvement in a nursing unit?

options.A: Making small, ongoing changes to solve identified problems and better patient care
options.B: Waiting for a major hospital disaster before updating any clinical rules
options.C: Keeping all nursing routines exactly the same for ten years
options.D: Punishing nurses whenever a patient complains about the food

explanation: You nailed it! Quality improvement is all about making steady, daily adjustments to our workflows to give our patients the best care possible.

question: Losing how much weight unintentionally in a single month is a major red flag for malnutrition?

options.A: Any weight loss at all
options.B: More than five percent
options.C: Ten pounds regardless of body size
options.D: Exactly one percent

explanation: Great job! Dropping over 5% of your body weight in a month is a serious warning sign that needs quick attention.

question: What is the VERY FIRST thing a nurse must do if a patient shows signs of a transfusion reaction?

options.A: Call the hospital maintenance team
options.B: Administer an oral pain reliever
options.C: Slow down the infusion pump rate
options.D: Stop the transfusion immediately

explanation: Safety first! Stopping the flow immediately keeps any more of the incompatible blood from entering their body. You're thinking like a real nurse!

question: A nurse accidentally pricks her finger with a hollow needle used to draw blood. What is the biggest worry?

options.A: Suffering from severe immediate muscle spasms
options.B: Developing an acute allergic reaction to latex
options.C: Developing localized skin necrosis on the finger
options.D: Exposure to bloodborne pathogens like HIV and Hepatitis

explanation: Hollow needles often hold infected blood inside them, which is why a prick poses a direct threat of viral transmission.

question: Why is it a bad idea to go grocery shopping on an empty stomach?

options.A: It makes non-essential snacks and food items look more tempting
options.B: It slows down the speed at which cashiers process payments
options.C: It causes sudden low blood pressure in the store aisle
options.D: It prevents the buyer from finding the correct grocery store

explanation: So true! Shopping while hungry always makes everything look delicious, leading to costly impulse buys you didn't budget for.

question: Which of these is NOT a good practice when designing a pie chart?

options.A: Grouping very small categories into an 'Other' slice
options.B: Including ten or more distinct slices for detail
options.C: Keeping the total sum strictly at 100 percent
options.D: Labeling percentages directly on the slices

explanation: You nailed it! Cramming ten or more slices into one pie creates a messy chart that nobody can read easily.

question: Why is it important for nurses to recognize the signs of the active dying phase?

options.A: To shift care goals toward maximum comfort and prepare the family
options.B: To start aggressive diagnostic blood tests right away
options.C: To transfer the patient back to the intensive care unit
options.D: To administer emergency resuscitation drugs immediately

explanation: Recognizing these signs helps us stop invasive procedures and focus entirely on keeping the patient peaceful and supporting their loved ones.

question: What happens during drug distribution in the body?

options.A: The liver breaks down the medicine into waste products
options.B: The gut absorbs a swallowed pill
options.C: The drug moves from the blood into various body tissues
options.D: The kidneys eliminate active drug molecules

explanation: Think of distribution as the drug's journey out of the bloodstream and into the body tissues where it's actually needed to work! You've got this.

question: Why are sympathetic preganglionic fibers usually shorter than the postganglionic fibers?

options.A: Because target organs are located directly next to the brain
options.B: Because they must travel long distances inside the spinal canal
options.C: Because they release hormones directly into the bloodstream
options.D: Because sympathetic ganglia sit close to the spinal cord

explanation: The relay stations (ganglia) hang out right next to the spinal cord in a chain. This means a short first hop (preganglionic) and a longer second hop (postganglionic) to reach the organs.

question: Which counseling approach works best when you want to help a teenager change their eating habits?

options.A: Handing them a strict, unchangeable 1,500-calorie diet chart
options.B: Directing their parents to control all food brought into the home
options.C: Asking open-ended questions to let the teen set personal goals
options.D: Warning them about future diseases until they agree to comply

explanation: You got it! Giving teens a voice and letting them choose their own goals makes them much more motivated to stick with healthy changes.

question: A patient is prescribed a metered-dose inhaler without a spacer and complains that the medicine just hits their throat. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Instruct the patient to hold their breath for five minutes after inhaling
options.B: Call the doctor to change the prescription to a skin patch
options.C: Advise the patient to obtain and use a spacer device to improve drug delivery
options.D: Tell the patient to swallow the medicine instead of breathing it in

explanation: Spacers act as a holding chamber that slows down the spray, preventing medication from depositing in the mouth and throat instead of the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h4)

question: Why is using frayed electrical cords dangerous?

options.A: They stop household light bulbs from working
options.B: Damaged cords pull too much electricity from the grid
options.C: Exposed wires can cause electric shock or fire
options.D: Frayed wires release toxic gases into the room

explanation: When insulation wears away, bare wires can spark against furniture or skin, causing burns or electrical shocks. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T4#GNS324_U6_T4_h7)

question: How should a nurse handle a cultural food taboo that limits a pregnant woman's protein intake?

options.A: Ignore the food taboo completely and focus only on vitamin supplements
options.B: Provide respectful education while suggesting nutritious local alternatives
options.C: Mock the cultural belief to force the patient into immediate compliance
options.D: Report the family to local community authorities for traditional practices

explanation: Respectful dialogue and culturally sensitive education work best to address harmful myths without alienating the patient or community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h5)

question: In research language, what is a 'sampling frame'?

options.A: A framework for writing up the final research report
options.B: The physical room where patient interviews take place
options.C: A complete list of everyone in the accessible population
options.D: The statistical formula used to calculate sample size

explanation: Think of a sampling frame as your phone book or registry list. It's the actual directory of names you draw your participants from!

question: Why is routine immunization considered a vital part of Primary Health Care?

options.A: It serves as a primary surgical cure for congenital heart defects
options.B: It is used exclusively to treat chronic lifestyle diseases in adults
options.C: It replaces the need for proper nutrition and clean drinking water
options.D: It actively prevents children from contracting dangerous, vaccine-preventable infectious diseases

explanation: Immunization is a powerful shield that stops deadly childhood infections before they can spread.

question: What does the clinical term 'polypharmacy' mean?

options.A: The delivery of drugs through an intravenous line
options.B: The concurrent use of multiple medications by a patient
options.C: The process of mixing liquid medicines with food
options.D: The manufacturing of generic drugs by large pharmacies

explanation: Polypharmacy simply means taking several medications at once. It's very common in older adults and increases the risk of side effects and dangerous drug interactions.

question: What is a common reason adolescent girls miss or drop out of school once they reach puberty?

options.A: Mandatory government laws prohibiting teenagers from studying science
options.B: Complete lack of interest in academic subjects after primary education
options.C: Sudden loss of intellectual capacity related to biological changes
options.D: Lack of private sanitation facilities and affordable menstrual products

explanation: Sadly, many girls miss classes because their schools lack clean, private toilets or affordable pads to manage their periods comfortably.

question: Which serious medical condition is a very common trigger for acute DIC?

options.A: Essential hypertension
options.B: Chronic osteoarthritis
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Severe sepsis

explanation: Severe infections and sepsis release a flood of inflammatory chemicals that accidentally trigger widespread clotting all over the body.

question: How do combined hormonal contraceptive pills mainly prevent pregnancy?

options.A: By creating a permanent blockage in the fallopian tubes
options.B: By destroying sperm cells on contact
options.C: By causing early shedding of the womb lining every week
options.D: By stopping ovulation and thickening cervical mucus

explanation: Well done! These hormones trick the body into not releasing an egg while also making it hard for sperm to swim through.

question: What is the main job of progesterone during pregnancy?

options.A: Relaxing the uterine muscle to prevent premature contractions
options.B: Lowering maternal blood pressure to protect the kidneys
options.C: Stimulating milk production in the maternal breasts
options.D: Triggering the onset of active labor at term

explanation: Progesterone keeps the uterus calm and relaxed (like a peaceful home) so the baby stays safe inside until it is fully ready for birth. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T5#GNS121_U6_T5_h6)

question: Which cells in the pancreas release insulin to lower your blood sugar after a meal?

options.A: Alpha cells
options.B: Delta cells
options.C: Acinar cells
options.D: Beta cells

explanation: Pancreatic beta cells are your body's sugar sweepers—they release insulin to help cells soak up glucose after you eat.

question: What is the main goal of Quality Assurance in nursing?

options.A: To punish staff who make mistakes
options.B: To increase the number of daily admissions
options.C: To reduce the cost of hospital drugs
options.D: To prevent care errors before they happen

explanation: You've got this! Quality assurance is all about staying a step ahead. Instead of waiting for a mistake, we use ongoing checks to keep our patients safe from the get-go.

question: What does the 'wearing-off' phenomenon mean for a patient taking Parkinson's medication?

options.A: The medication loses its effectiveness before the next scheduled dose is due.
options.B: The patient develops a permanent allergic reaction to the drug ingredients.
options.C: The patient no longer requires any treatment due to spontaneous recovery.
options.D: The dosage must be permanently reduced to prevent severe liver toxicity.

explanation: It's like a battery running low before you can plug it in. The medicine wears off too early, causing the patient's symptoms to return right before it's time for their next pill.

question: What temperature range is known as the 'danger zone' where food safety is at risk?

options.A: Above 100°C
options.B: Between 0°C and 10°C
options.C: Below freezing point
options.D: Between 5°C and 60°C

explanation: Correct! Bad bacteria multiply super fast when food hangs out in this 5°C to 60°C danger zone.

question: Why did governments start using public insurance to fund home health care programs?

options.A: To discourage families from taking care of relatives at home
options.B: To reduce the high financial burden of long-term hospital stays
options.C: To completely replace traditional doctors with visiting nurses
options.D: To stop the construction of new community health clinics

explanation: Governments figured out that home care is usually much cheaper than keeping patients in acute care hospital wards for weeks of recovery.

question: Tracking a patient's fluid intake and output mainly helps you evaluate what?

options.A: Lung capacity and oxygen levels
options.B: Muscle strength in the lower limbs
options.C: Kidney function and hydration status
options.D: The patient's daily calorie intake

explanation: Checking what goes in versus what comes out is a brilliant way to see if the kidneys are doing their job and if the patient is well-hydrated.

question: What is a 'steroid flare' that some patients experience after a joint injection?

options.A: An immediate permanent cure of all joint stiffness
options.B: A sudden rash spread all over the patient's face
options.C: A temporary increase in joint pain before the medication starts working
options.D: A permanent allergic reaction requiring emergency surgery

explanation: Some patients feel extra soreness for a day or two when steroid crystals irritate the joint before calming down. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T9#GNS125_U3_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of microbial surveillance in public health?

options.A: Evaluating nursing staff performance
options.B: Treating individual patients in a clinic
options.C: Tracking and analyzing disease trends
options.D: Manufacturing new antibiotics for hospitals

explanation: Surveillance focuses on watching data across populations to spot trends and manage health risks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h1)

question: A home health registered nurse notices a sudden worsening of a patient's heart failure symptoms. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Wait until the scheduled visit next week to document it
options.B: Discharge the patient from home care services immediately
options.C: Report the clinical changes to the primary physician
options.D: Ask the physical therapist to adjust the cardiac medications

explanation: Registered nurses must promptly report significant changes in patient status to the attending doctor to prevent avoidable hospital admissions. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T4#GNS324_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which organ is primarily responsible for filtering and excreting water-soluble drug waste?

options.A: Kidneys
options.B: Lungs
options.C: Spleen
options.D: Skin

explanation: Your kidneys are your body's ultimate filters. They continuously clean your blood and flush out water-soluble drug breakdown products through your urine.

question: What is the main goal of mental health promotion?

options.A: Building positive emotional strength and well-being
options.B: Treating severe psychiatric disorders with medication
options.C: Managing acute crisis behaviors in the emergency room
options.D: Discharging stable patients back into the community

explanation: Mental health promotion focuses on enhancing overall emotional well-being and psychological strength rather than treating existing illness. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T1#GNS314_U5_T1_h1)

question: Which powerful diuretic is most commonly used to quickly clear fluid from a patient's lungs in acute heart failure?

options.A: Spironolactone
options.B: Mannitol
options.C: Furosemide
options.D: Hydrochlorothiazide

explanation: Furosemide is a true workhorse in the ward! It's a loop diuretic that quickly removes extra fluid through urine, giving relief to patients struggling to breathe.

question: What is the main job of psychological defense mechanisms?

options.A: To permanently cure chronic depression
options.B: To improve physical muscle strength under stress
options.C: To shield the mind from sudden emotional pain and anxiety
options.D: To increase conscious awareness of personal faults

explanation: Think of defense mechanisms as a mental shock absorber. They protect us unconsciously when stress or bad news feels too heavy to process all at once.

question: A patient tells you: 'My chest feels tight since this morning.' Where should you document this exact statement?

options.A: Discharge planning and social history
options.B: Objective physical examination findings
options.C: Past medical history and surgical background
options.D: Chief complaint and history of present illness

explanation: Active symptoms that patients report themselves always go right into the chief complaint and history of present illness sections.

question: Which gland releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone to trigger the female reproductive cycle?

options.A: The anterior pituitary gland
options.B: The adrenal cortex
options.C: The hypothalamus
options.D: The posterior pituitary gland

explanation: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone is synthesized and released by the hypothalamus in the brain to kick off the hormonal cascade. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h1)

question: How does a newborn baby naturally receive passive immunity from their mother?

options.A: Through breast milk and across the placenta
options.B: By developing mild infections in the nursery
options.C: By receiving routine infant vaccinations at birth
options.D: Through exposure to sunlight during infancy

explanation: You nailed it! Mums pass helpful antibodies to their babies across the placenta during pregnancy and through breast milk after birth.

question: Which social factor is consistently proven to help young girls delay marriage and early childbearing?

options.A: Traditional community ceremonies
options.B: Living in an urban city center
options.C: Access to formal education
options.D: Employment in the agricultural sector

explanation: Education is a powerful tool! When girls stay in school, they gain knowledge, open up better life opportunities, and naturally delay marriage and childbearing.

question: Once an expectorant thins out the respiratory mucus, what helps sweep it up toward the throat?

options.A: They absorb the excess fluid so the lungs stay completely dry
options.B: They dissolve the chemical bonds holding the phlegm together
options.C: They sweep the loosened mucus upward toward the throat
options.D: They produce more thick mucus to trap remaining dust particles

explanation: Meet the cilia—tiny hair-like structures in your airways that wave together like a stadium crowd to push that loosened mucus right up and out!

question: What happens during a uterine perforation?

options.A: An instrument punctures the wall of the uterus.
options.B: The uterine muscle permanently stops contracting.
options.C: Blood clots block the fallopian tubes completely.
options.D: The cervix fails to dilate during surgery.

explanation: Simply put, 'perforation' means a hole. It occurs when a surgical instrument accidentally pokes through the muscular wall of the uterus.

question: What do we call a pregnancy where a mother is carrying two or more babies at the same time?

options.A: Singleton pregnancy
options.B: Ectopic pregnancy
options.C: Multiple pregnancy
options.D: Molar pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! A multiple pregnancy just means carrying more than one fetus—like twins, triplets, or more. You've got this!

question: What is your main role as a nurse during family planning counseling?

options.A: To enforce government population targets
options.B: To convince every young person to get sterilized
options.C: To provide clear information so the client can choose freely
options.D: To choose the best contraceptive method for the client

explanation: Correct! As nurses, we guide and educate without forcing our personal choices on our patients.

question: A patient stops taking their prescribed tuberculosis medication because it makes them feel nauseated every morning. What kind of barrier does this represent?

options.A: Financial barrier
options.B: Language barrier
options.C: Transportation barrier
options.D: Side effect barrier

explanation: Adverse drug reactions such as nausea are common side effects that discourage patients from continuing their treatment unless managed properly. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why does a drop in local currency value make medications so much more expensive?

options.A: Doctors start prescribing more expensive brands
options.B: Governments place heavy taxes on local pharmacies
options.C: Many essential drugs and raw materials are imported
options.D: Local factories stop producing tablets entirely

explanation: Spot on! Because we import a lot of our medicines and raw ingredients, a weaker currency means it costs much more to bring them into the country.

question: A patient develops severe belly pain and a hard, rigid abdomen a few hours after a paracentesis. What could this mean?

options.A: Internal bleeding or bowel perforation
options.B: A mild allergic reaction to the dressing
options.C: Normal healing of the puncture wound
options.D: Successful removal of all ascites fluid

explanation: A hard, painful belly is a red flag! It can point to a serious issue like internal bleeding or an accidental nick in the bowel.

question: Why must Nigerian nurses understand local health-seeking behaviors?

options.A: To eliminate the need for community health outreach programs
options.B: To prove that traditional medicine has no value in society
options.C: To provide culturally sensitive care and bridge traditional and modern practices
options.D: To force every patient to completely abandon their religious beliefs

explanation: Spot on! When we respect cultural beliefs and money realities, we can build trust and safely guide patients to the best medical care.

question: Why do researchers clean their data before running statistics?

options.A: To reduce the number of participants needed for the study
options.B: To catch entry mistakes and prevent false research results
options.C: To get extra funding from the hospital research committee
options.D: To make the research report shorter and easier to print

explanation: Data cleaning is like double-checking your medication dosage math—it catches errors early so your final results are accurate and safe.

question: What does the term 'ex post facto' mean?

options.A: Before the intervention
options.B: Randomly assigned
options.C: During the experiment
options.D: After the fact

explanation: Easy peasy! 'Ex post facto' simply means 'after the fact'. The event has already happened, and we are looking backward to figure out what might have caused it.

question: When should you, as the nurse, do your final dosage calculation?

options.A: Only when the pharmacist calls
options.B: Right before giving the drug
options.C: After a bad reaction happens
options.D: During your annual nursing review

explanation: Always double-check your math right before administration. It is your last chance to catch mistakes before the drug enters the patient's body.

question: Why is knowing research classifications important for evidence-based nursing?

options.A: It removes the need to talk directly with patients
options.B: It guarantees that hospital budgets will increase
options.C: It forces nurses to memorize difficult medical terminology
options.D: It helps nurses judge the strength and quality of evidence

explanation: That's right! Understanding how studies are grouped lets nurses evaluate whether a piece of evidence is strong enough to safely change patient care. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h7)

question: A patient is unconscious and unable to swallow safely. What is a main reason to insert an NG tube?

options.A: To permanently cure the underlying brain injury
options.B: To provide safe enteral nutrition and hydration
options.C: To prevent the patient from moving in bed
options.D: To replace the need for routine oral hygiene care

explanation: If a patient can't swallow safely, we still need to feed them! An NG tube lets us deliver food and water straight to the stomach without choking risks.

question: A patient develops scar tissue inside her uterus after a complicated D&C (dilation and curettage) procedure. What is this condition called?

options.A: Endometrial hyperplasia
options.B: Asherman's syndrome
options.C: Adenomyosis
options.D: Uterine didelphys

explanation: You nailed it! Asherman's syndrome refers to intrauterine adhesions or scars that typically form following surgeries inside the uterine cavity.

question: Why do heart muscle cells packed with so many mitochondria?

options.A: To store excess calcium ions required for action potential plateaus
options.B: To manufacture contractile proteins like actin and myosin on demand
options.C: To continuously produce large amounts of ATP needed for constant pumping
options.D: To regulate the body's overall systemic blood pressure levels

explanation: Your heart never takes a break! It needs a massive, non-stop supply of ATP power plants (mitochondria) to keep beating 24/7.

question: How do nurses act as a bridge in disaster response networks?

options.A: By taking over the administrative duties of local government chairmen
options.B: By managing military transport logistics during emergency evacuations
options.C: By negotiating international financial loans for hospital construction
options.D: By connecting clinical bedside care with public health administration and planning

explanation: Nurses see what patients need firsthand, helping connect hands-on care with the bigger picture of public health planning.

question: How does a nurse apply the principle of justice on a busy hospital ward?

options.A: By ignoring minor complaints from elderly clients to focus on wealthy individuals
options.B: By spending the entire shift caring only for clients who pay extra hospital fees
options.C: By providing equal and fair quality care to every assigned client regardless of background
options.D: By refusing to admit clients who belong to a different religious group

explanation: Justice means treating all clients fairly and equitably without bias or discrimination based on their social status. [learn more](GST321_U10_T5#GST321_U10_T5_h2)

question: What natural monthly bodily change affects an adolescent girl's need for extra iron?

options.A: Ovulation
options.B: Menarche
options.C: The growth spurt
options.D: Pubarche

explanation: Spot on! Menarche (the start of monthly periods) means the body needs to replenish its iron stores regularly. You're doing great!

question: Which of these is NOT a right that patients keep while on psychiatric parole?

options.A: The right to completely ignore court-ordered treatment without consequences
options.B: The right to give informed consent for general healthcare
options.C: The right to access legal help and representation
options.D: The right to be treated with dignity and professional respect

explanation: You nailed it! Parole comes with conditions—ignoring your treatment plan means breaking those conditions, which leads back to clinical or legal intervention.

question: Why do healthcare providers use the word 'spectrum' when talking about autism?

options.A: It measures the exact intelligence level of the patient
options.B: It indicates how quickly the condition can be cured
options.C: It shows that symptoms vary widely in severity and presentation
options.D: It proves the condition changes completely every few years

explanation: Think of a rainbow! The 'spectrum' shows that no two autistic people are exactly alike—they experience traits and challenges in vastly different ways.

question: Which major structural change happens in the lungs of someone with emphysema?

options.A: Thickening of the pleural space with fibrous scar tissue
options.B: Destruction of alveolar walls and loss of lung elasticity
options.C: Permanent blockage of the main pulmonary artery by clots
options.D: Excessive production of watery fluid inside the pleural cavity

explanation: You got it! Emphysema breaks down the walls of the air sacs and destroys the elastic fibers, making it hard for the lungs to bounce back when breathing out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: What type of germ causes trichomoniasis?

options.A: A bacterium
options.B: A protozoan
options.C: A fungus
options.D: A prion

explanation: Trichomoniasis is caused by a tiny, single-celled parasite (a protozoan) that loves to cause irritation and unusual discharge.

question: Which substance is most widely available and socially accepted among young people?

options.A: Methamphetamine
options.B: Alcohol
options.C: Heroin
options.D: Cocain

explanation: Correct! Alcohol is the most commonly consumed and socially tolerated substance among adolescents, both globally and right here at home.

question: How does the 'revolving' part of a DRF actually work in practice?

options.A: Unsold expired drugs are returned to manufacturers for full cash refunds
options.B: Donors inject new capital into the pharmacy every single month
options.C: Money collected from drug sales is used to buy fresh stock
options.D: Profits from drug sales are returned to the government treasury

explanation: Spot on! Patients buy drugs, that money goes back into the kitty, and the pharmacy uses it to buy the next batch. It is a continuous loop that keeps the pharmacy stocked.

question: Why do nurses need to understand the basic chemistry of food nutrients?

options.A: It determines the physical weight and height requirements for clinical admissions
options.B: It explains how the body transforms food into cellular fuel and structural components
options.C: It allows nurses to calculate exact retail food prices for hospital kitchens
options.D: It helps nurses prescribe specific synthetic chemical medications for patients

explanation: Knowing how nutrients are built helps you understand digestion and why our bodies need a mix of different foods to stay healthy.

question: Which of these is NOT a typical problem caused by poorly planned, excessive protein intake?

options.A: Potential for chronic constipation due to low fiber
options.B: Extra workload for the kidneys
options.C: Immediate development of type 1 diabetes
options.D: Increased risk of dehydration

question: A client vomits twenty minutes after taking her emergency contraceptive pill. What should you do?

options.A: Ignore the vomiting because it has no effect on the medication
options.B: Consult the provider to see if a repeat dose is needed
options.C: Give her a high dose of intravenous antibiotics immediately
options.D: Tell her the pill failed and she must schedule surgery

explanation: If she vomits shortly after taking the pill (within two hours), her body might not have absorbed the medicine. Always check with the clinician if she needs another dose!

question: In the 'method of authority,' why do people accept a piece of information as true?

options.A: The patient insists that the treatment works
options.B: The information comes from a respected or credible source
options.C: The data was gathered through personal dreams
options.D: The procedure takes less than five minutes to complete

explanation: This method relies on trust in someone perceived as an expert, like a senior consultant or an established textbook.

question: As a nurse, why is your role in medication administration so important?

options.A: Prescribing the correct dosage based on lab results
options.B: Manufacturing safe chemical compounds for hospital use
options.C: Acting as the final safety barrier before the drug reaches the patient
options.D: Selling pharmaceutical supplies to hospital wards

explanation: You are the last line of defense! By double-checking the order and the patient right before giving the drug, you catch mistakes that might have slipped through earlier. Great job keeping patients safe!

question: Why is continuous quality improvement important after putting a team care plan in place?

options.A: To punish team members who make minor documentation errors
options.B: To increase the paperwork burden for community nurses
options.C: To identify weaknesses and update processes for better patient results
options.D: To prove to the government that the clinic has extra funding

explanation: Brilliant! Quality improvement is all about learning and growing so we can give our patients better care every single day.

question: Why might a family quickly arrange a marriage for a teenage daughter out of fear of neighborhood gossip?

options.A: To satisfy mandatory school attendance laws
options.B: To protect the family's social reputation and perceived honor
options.C: To secure a government housing subsidy for newlyweds
options.D: To comply with international public health guidelines

explanation: Spot on! Fear of community gossip and shame often pushes families to use early marriage as a fast way to guard their social standing.

question: Why should nurses care about a patient's social background when talking about reproductive health?

options.A: It ensures the patient will always follow medical advice
options.B: It allows nurses to change national laws regarding healthcare
options.C: It replaces the need for a physical medical examination
options.D: It helps nurses see the real-world barriers affecting patient choices

explanation: You got it! Understanding social factors helps you see the real struggles a patient faces in getting care, making you a more empathetic nurse.

question: What does the back part of the pituitary gland (posterior pituitary) actually do?

options.A: It stores and releases hormones made by the hypothalamus.
options.B: It makes growth hormone and prolactin every single day.
options.C: It controls blood sugar levels using special insulin cells.

question: At what centimeter of cervical dilation does the alert line on the partograph traditionally start?

options.A: 10 cm
options.B: 7 cm
options.C: 4 cm
options.D: 1 cm

explanation: Active labour officially kicks off at 4 cm dilation, which is right where the alert line begins on your chart.

question: What is the most reliable, go-to test used in labs to check for chlamydia and gonorrhea?

options.A: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
options.B: Microscopic wet mount preparation
options.C: Nucleic acid amplification testing
options.D: Complete blood cell count analysis

question: Which skin change is a classic sign of long-term chronic venous insufficiency?

options.A: Shiny, hairless skin with thick toenails on the toes
options.B: Painful black sores right on the tips of the heels
options.C: Pale, cool skin that turns white instantly when lifted
options.D: Brownish skin discoloration and irritation around the ankles

explanation: High pressure in the lower leg veins forces tiny red blood cells to leak out into the skin. When they break down, they leave behind a rusty brown stain called hemosiderin.

question: Why is severe, sudden hypotension dangerous for a patient?

options.A: Sudden thickening of the heart muscle walls
options.B: Inadequate perfusion and oxygenation of vital organs
options.C: Immediate rupture of peripheral veins in the arms
options.D: Permanent blockage of the major coronary arteries

explanation: If blood pressure crashes, there isn't enough pushing power to deliver life-giving oxygen to vital organs like the brain and kidneys.

question: What type of protective equipment is recommended when working with harsh chemical disinfectants that might splash?

options.A: Paper surgical caps and cloth masks
options.B: Open sandals and thin cotton gowns
options.C: Sterile surgical gloves and boots
options.D: Face shields and waterproof aprons

explanation: Face shields protect the eyes and mucous membranes from chemical splashes, while waterproof aprons protect clothing and skin. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h7)

question: You tell a nervous patient, 'I am not rushed at all,' but you keep checking your watch and eyeing the door. What will they believe?

options.A: The spoken words because nurses are always honest
options.B: That the clock is broken and the nurse is relaxed
options.C: The non-verbal cue that the nurse is in a rush
options.D: Both messages equally without any confusion

explanation: Spot on! When words and body language clash, patients almost always trust what your body is showing them.

question: When working in community health, what does the helpful acronym 'IEC' stand for?

options.A: Infection, Environment, and Control
options.B: Information, Education, and Communication
options.C: Immunization, Evaluation, and Care
options.D: Investigation, Education, and Counseling

explanation: IEC stands for Information, Education, and Communication. You'll use these three core strategies every day to promote health and prevent disease in your communities!

question: What does a 'null hypothesis' usually say about two groups being compared?

options.A: The first group always has a higher score
options.B: The second group received a better treatment
options.C: There is no real difference between them
options.D: There are not enough patients in the study

explanation: The null hypothesis assumes a boring baseline: that your new treatment didn't actually do anything special and the groups are essentially the same.

question: What is the name of the layer of cells that clings directly to the released egg upon ovulation?

options.A: Zona pellucida
options.B: Endometrium
options.C: Corona radiata
options.D: Myometrium

question: Which body parts are included in the appendicular region?

options.A: Thorax and abdomen

options.C: Upper and lower limbs
options.D: Head and neck

explanation: The appendicular region contains all the bones and soft tissues of the upper and lower extremities. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why is just counting calories often not enough when caring for a patient's nutrition?

options.A: Calories change drastically depending on the time of day a meal is served
options.B: Calories do not reflect whether the body can actually absorb and use the nutrients
options.C: Patient metabolism makes calorie tracking completely impossible in a hospital
options.D: Processed foods always have lower calorie counts than raw food items

explanation: Great thinking! A meal can be packed with calories yet lack the vital building blocks our cells and tissues need to heal.

question: What does 'myelosuppression' mean?

options.A: A sudden swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck
options.B: An infection located directly on the outer layer of the skin
options.C: The suppression of blood cell production in the bone marrow
options.D: The overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow

explanation: Big medical word, simple meaning! It just means cancer treatments slow down bone marrow activity, leading to low blood counts. You're learning fast!

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to handle confounding when designing a study?

options.A: Matching cases and controls for confounding traits
options.B: Intentionally falsifying data to match the hypothesis
options.C: Randomizing participants if possible
options.D: Restricting the study to specific age groups

explanation: Never fake data! Falsifying results is serious scientific misconduct. We control confounders through smart study design instead.

question: Why is Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) ranked as the least effective way to control hazards?

options.A: It depends on human behavior and can easily fail or be worn incorrectly
options.B: It is always too expensive for companies to purchase in bulk
options.C: It completely removes the hazard from the physical environment
options.D: It increases the physical speed at which employees perform tasks

explanation: PPE is super important, but it's a last line of defense because if a worker forgets to wear it or wears it wrongly, they are still exposed to danger!

question: What is the main benefit of keeping a clear audit trail in a Drug Revolving Fund?

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do when helping someone with a fresh thermal burn?

question: What does the FIFO stock rotation rule stand for?
